questions.question: Drinking water at school is a ___.
questions.explain: Water is something your body must have to live, so it is a need. A toy or game is fun but you do not need it to stay healthy.

questions.question: You have 50 cents. A pencil costs 30 cents. Can you buy it?
questions.explain: You compare 50 with 30. Since 50 is bigger than 30, you have enough. The trap is adding them together instead of just comparing.

questions.question: You want to buy a chocolate bar for 50 cents. You have 4 dimes. Is it enough?
questions.explain: 4 dimes is 40 cents, which is less than 50, so it is not enough. More coins does not always mean more money.

questions.question: You have 60 cents. You spend 25 cents on a pencil. How much is left to save?
questions.explain: You take 25 away from 60, which gives 35 cents to save. The trap is keeping the 60 and forgetting to take the 25 away.

questions.question: Mia has 75 cents. She buys a pencil for 50 cents for school. How much is left?
questions.explain: You take 50 away from 75, which gives 25 cents left. Do not count the 50 you spent as still being in your hand.

questions.question: Sam wants to buy two stickers. Each costs 20 cents. Sam has 3 dimes. Can he buy both?
questions.explain: 3 dimes is 30 cents, but two stickers cost 40 cents. 30 is less than 40, so it is not enough.

questions.question: Zoe has 80 cents. She saves 30 cents for a book. She spends the rest on a lollipop. How much is the lollipop?
questions.explain: You take 30 away from 80, which gives 50 cents for the lollipop. Do not add the 30 back in after taking it out.

questions.question: Ben has 90 cents. He buys a notebook for 40 cents. Then he buys a comic for 30 cents. How much is left to save?
questions.explain: First take 40 from 90 to get 50, then take 30 from 50 to get 20 cents left. You must take both purchases away, not just one.

questions.question: You have 50 cents. You spend 35 on a sandwich. You want to save 15. Is it enough to do both?
questions.explain: You take 35 away from 50, which gives exactly 15 cents to save. The trap is thinking the 35 you spent is still in your pocket.

questions.question: Ava has 60 cents. She buys a pen for 25 cents for school. Then she sees a card for 40 cents. Can she buy the card?
questions.explain: You take 25 away from 60 to get 35 cents. The card costs 40, and 35 is less than 40, so it is not enough.

questions.question: Tom says: I had 50 cents. I spent 30 on a need. I still have 50 cents to save. What went wrong?
questions.explain: Tom still counts the 30 he spent as if it is in his pocket. After spending 30 of 50, he only has 20 left, not 50.

questions.question: Leo has 2 quarters and 1 dime. His class needs a glue stick that costs 55 cents. Can he buy it?
options: Yes, and he still has 60 cents.
No, 3 coins is less than 55 cents.
No, a glue stick is just a want.
questions.explain: 2 quarters and 1 dime make 60 cents, and 60 is more than 55, so yes. Count what the coins are worth, not how many coins there are.

questions.question: Ben has 5 nickels in his pocket. Milk for his school lunch costs 50 cents. Can he buy the milk?
options: No, milk is a want, so he skips it.
Yes, 5 coins is more than 50 cents.
Yes, and he can still save 25 cents.
questions.explain: Nickels count by fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 cents, which is less than 50. Having more coins does not always mean having more money.

questions.question: Ivy has 3 quarters. She owes the library 55 cents for a late book. A bracelet at the store costs 30 cents.
options: Buy the bracelet first, it is a need.
Pay the library, then save 20 cents.
Pay the library and buy the bracelet.
She cannot pay, 3 coins is under 55.
questions.explain: 3 quarters make 75 cents. The library money is a need, so pay 55 cents first; that leaves 20 cents, which is not enough for the 30-cent bracelet.
